network.overall_strategy: This evidence-qualified network contains 10 distinct conditional reaction sequences, not 10 independently demonstrated prebiotic mechanisms. It combines aromatic-aldehyde Strecker chemistry, phenylalanine hydroxylation, aromatic-keto-acid reductive amination, cyanide-mediated hydantoin formation, and decarboxylative nitrogen transfer. The aromatic supply bottleneck remains explicit: formation of phenylacetylene under the specified environmental conditions is uncertain, while 4-hydroxyphenylacetaldehyde, phenylpyruvate, and 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate are conditional boundary feedstocks with no established prebiotic synthesis in the supplied evidence. No invented reaction closes those gaps. Consequently, this is a complete conditional graph, not a demonstrated synthesis of tyrosine entirely from simple feedstocks. Shared modules generate the 10 reaction-distinct pathways without implying 10 independent reaction families. Molecular oxygen is neither supplied nor required by the proposed net reactions; the oxygen-free radical-hydroxylation variants nevertheless remain experimentally unverified. Oxidizing and reducing modules require separate compartments. Iron(II) hydroxide is represented as a consumed reductant, not a catalyst. The extreme-temperature silica route is excluded because its 1223–1323 K conditions exceed the specified environmental windows. Neutral molecular formulas represent acid-base families, and stereochemically unspecified amino-acid structures denote racemic products. Boundary inputs have environment_formed set to null. Reaction outputs describe target-forming channels and selected competing products, not an exhaustive inventory of degradation products.

reactions.name: Conditional high-energy assembly of phenylacetylene from acetylene

conditions.temperature: 300–370 K bulk gas; nonthermal excitation required
conditions.other: Locally reducing, oxygen-free acetylene-rich gas subjected to electrical discharge; products must subsequently enter an aqueous reservoir. This is not a thermal reaction at the stated bulk temperature.

reactions.mechanism: Unresolved radical oligomerization, cyclization, and dehydrogenation. The selected product channel has the formal balance 4 C2H2 -> C8H6 + H2; this is not an elementary mechanism or a yield prediction.
reactions.reasoning: Low confidence under the specified conditions. High-energy hydrocarbon chemistry can supply phenylacetylene, but the supplied report primarily supports mixed aromatic production by high-temperature or discharge chemistry, not selective conversion at this bulk temperature (Friedmann & Miller, 1969; Stephen-Sherwood & Oró, 1973). This low-temperature, nonthermal implementation is speculative and explicitly represents an unresolved aromatic-supply bottleneck. Benzene, other aromatics, and refractory oligomers would compete.

reactions.name: Sulfur-assisted conversion of phenylacetylene to a thioaldehyde

conditions.pressure: Approximately 1 atm in a gas-retaining aqueous setting
conditions.other: Anoxic sulfide-bearing water; proposed pH 7–9; photochemical initiation can contribute to radical hydrosulfidation. The thioaldehyde is transient rather than an assumed accumulated reservoir.

reactions.mechanism: Hydrogen-sulfide addition to the alkyne, with the productive regioisomer passing through an enethiol/thioaldehyde manifold.
reactions.reasoning: The sulfur-assisted phenylacetylene-to-phenylacetaldehyde sequence is supported by Friedmann & Miller (1969), who describe nucleophilic and radical H2S addition followed by thioaldehyde hydrolysis. The isolated-node representation resolves that reported intermediate class but does not establish its concentration or every elementary step. This edge belongs to the phenylalanine arm; it does not explain the reported minor tyrosine branch or install a para hydroxyl group.

reactions.name: Hydrolysis of phenylacetothialdehyde

conditions.other: Aqueous trapping of the transient sulfur-containing intermediate; sulfide speciation depends on pH.

reactions.mechanism: Water addition and sulfur–oxygen exchange convert the thioaldehyde to phenylacetaldehyde while releasing hydrogen sulfide.
reactions.reasoning: Supported as part of the sulfur-mediated aldehyde-forming sequence described by Friedmann & Miller (1969). Regeneration of sulfide is chemically required by this hydrolysis, not added to manufacture network connectivity. Competing sulfur oligomerization and aldehyde loss remain unquantified.

reactions.name: Strecker formation of phenylalanine aminonitrile

conditions.pressure: Approximately 1 atm in a covered or gas-retaining pool
conditions.other: Approximately pH 8.3; locally concentrated aldehyde, ammonia, and cyanide; protection from prolonged destructive irradiation.

reactions.mechanism: Aldehyde–ammonia condensation establishes an imine/iminium pool, followed by cyanide addition to produce the racemic aminonitrile.
reactions.reasoning: Supported by the phenylacetaldehyde Strecker sequence of Friedmann & Miller (1969). Stephen-Sherwood & Oró (1973) report pH 8.3, 80 °C, and a 20.4% phenylalanine yield for the overall relevant sequence; that number is not assigned to this isolated aminonitrile-forming edge. Cyanohydrin formation, aldehyde condensation, and HCN volatilization compete.

reactions.name: Hydrolysis of phenylalanine aminonitrile
agents: Hydronium ions for acid-catalyzed nitrile hydrolysis

conditions.other: Proposed acidic hydrolysis stage, approximately pH 1–2, spatially or temporally separated from Strecker formation. Required residence time is not established for the proposed natural setting.

reactions.mechanism: Sequential nitrile hydration through an amide gives phenylalanine and ammonia/ammonium; two water equivalents are consumed in the neutral-species net balance.
reactions.reasoning: Aminonitrile hydrolysis is the established completion of the Strecker sequence used by Friedmann & Miller (1969). The specified mild-temperature acidic implementation is a proposed environmental realization, not a verified reproduction of their complete workup. Hydrolysis and survival of the aromatic aminonitrile are kinetic bottlenecks; racemic phenylalanine is expected.

reactions.name: Conditional oxygen-free Fenton hydroxylation of phenylalanine
agents: Dissolved Fe(II)/Fe(III) redox couple, with Fe(III) generated in situ

conditions.other: Oxygen-free, mildly acidic microenvironment; trace peroxide supplied separately; limited exposure followed by removal from the radical-generating zone. Iron precipitation can interrupt turnover.

reactions.mechanism: Fe(II) activates peroxide to form hydroxyl radicals. Radical addition to the aromatic ring gives hydroxycyclohexadienyl radicals. Oxidation by in-situ-generated Fe(III), rather than molecular oxygen, is proposed to restore aromaticity. The outputs represent competing positional-isomer channels, not equal product yields.
reactions.reasoning: Phenylalanine hydroxylation to ortho-, meta-, and para-tyrosine is experimentally established using hydroxyl radicals (Kaur et al., 1988), and its possible prebiotic relevance was discussed by Weber & Miller (1981). However, the selected strictly oxygen-free iron-cycling implementation is speculative; the cited observations do not establish its yield under these conditions. Para selectivity is absent, and further oxidation of the products can erase accumulation. No reported total tyrosine yield is interpreted as a para-tyrosine yield.

reactions.name: Conditional oxygen-free UV/peroxide hydroxylation of phenylalanine

conditions.other: Oxygen-free shallow water exposed to peroxide-absorbing UV wavelengths, approximately 200–280 nm where locally transmitted; low conversion and short exposure are favored over prolonged irradiation.

reactions.mechanism: Peroxide photolysis produces hydroxyl radicals. Aromatic addition followed by radical- or peroxide-mediated rearomatization is proposed to yield a mixture of hydroxyphenylalanines without an O2-dependent step.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative oxygen-free implementation of established hydroxyl-radical attack on phenylalanine (Kaur et al., 1988; Weber & Miller, 1981). The supplied studies do not demonstrate this exact UV/peroxide reaction under anoxia. Radical termination, side-chain oxidation, and destruction of newly formed tyrosine may dominate. This is a different radical-generation variant from rxn_006, not a separate proven prebiotic reaction family.

reactions.name: Conditional Strecker formation of tyrosine aminonitrile

conditions.pressure: Approximately 1 atm in a gas-retaining setting
conditions.other: Proposed pH 8–9; concentrated conditional aromatic-aldehyde feedstock; minimize aldehyde oxidation and self-condensation.

reactions.mechanism: Imine formation from 4-hydroxyphenylacetaldehyde and ammonia, followed by cyanide addition, produces the racemic aromatic aminonitrile.
reactions.reasoning: Chemically reasonable but speculative as a prebiotic tyrosine route. It extends the demonstrated aromatic-aldehyde Strecker chemistry of Friedmann & Miller (1969). The supplied report explicitly does not verify 4-hydroxyphenylacetaldehyde as the intermediate in their minor tyrosine branch. Its para-hydroxylated aromatic skeleton is therefore an unresolved boundary assumption, and the historical tyrosine yield cannot be assigned to this edge.

reactions.name: Conditional hydrolysis of tyrosine aminonitrile
agents: Hydronium ions for acid-catalyzed nitrile hydrolysis

conditions.other: Proposed pH 1–2 hydrolysis stage; subsequently cool and change pH if product precipitation is desired. Aromatic-substrate residence time and recovery require measurement.

reactions.mechanism: Nitrile hydration through an amide intermediate yields racemic para-tyrosine and ammonia/ammonium.
reactions.reasoning: Established transformation class, but the specific mild prebiotic implementation is speculative. Friedmann & Miller (1969) support an overall sulfur/Strecker route yielding a minor amount of tyrosine, not this independently characterized intermediate sequence. Nitrile hydrolysis may be slow within the permitted thermal window, and tyrosine recovery cannot be assumed quantitative.

reactions.name: Iron(II)-hydroxide-driven reductive amination of phenylpyruvate
agents: Freshly precipitated Fe(OH)2, consumed as a stoichiometric reductant

conditions.other: Oxygen-free alkaline geothermal pool; pH 9–11; high ammonia loading, approximately 0.375–1.5 M as an experimental concentration range rather than an established natural inventory.

reactions.mechanism: Ammonia adds to the keto group to establish an imine pool, which is reduced using Fe(II)-derived electrons. Two Fe(II) equivalents are oxidized per amino acid in the idealized balance. FeOOH represents a bookkeeping Fe(III) oxidation-product end member, not a demonstrated unique mineral phase.
reactions.reasoning: Aromatic-keto-acid reductive amination is supported by Huber & Wächtershäuser (2003), with aromatic amino-acid outcomes summarized by Milner-White & Russell (2008). Fe(OH)2 is not treated as a catalytic source of unlimited reducing equivalents. The major limitations are the unestablished prebiotic origin of phenylpyruvate, high ammonia demand, and uncertain oxidation-product mineralogy.

reactions.name: Iron(II)-hydroxide-driven reductive amination of 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate
agents: Freshly precipitated Fe(OH)2, consumed as a stoichiometric reductant

conditions.other: Oxygen-free alkaline pool; pH 9–11; concentrated ammonia, potentially approaching 1.5 M; physically separated from peroxide-generating chemistry.

reactions.mechanism: Imine formation at the alpha-keto group followed by two-electron reduction gives tyrosine. Fe(II) is consumed; the displayed ferric oxyhydroxide is an idealized oxidation-product sink.
reactions.reasoning: This is the best-supported terminal conversion in the keto-acid branch (Huber & Wächtershäuser, 2003). Reports of aromatic amino-acid yields up to approximately 50% are secondary summaries, not a verified tyrosine-specific yield transferable to this setting (Milner-White & Russell, 2008). The route remains precursor-limited because no supplied study establishes prebiotic production of 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate. High ammonia concentrations and mineral passivation are additional bottlenecks.

reactions.name: Conditional nickel/H2 reductive amination of 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate
agents: Nickel on silica-alumina as an experimental mineral-interface analogue

conditions.pressure: H2-bearing gas atmosphere; pressure dependence for this aromatic substrate is unmeasured
conditions.other: Approximately pH 8; 6–150 mM total ammonia/ammonium as a screening range; no peroxide or molecular oxygen. Natural assembly and activity of an equivalent supported nickel material are not established.

reactions.mechanism: Surface-activated hydrogen reduces a keto-acid-derived imine. Direct carbonyl reduction to 4-hydroxyphenyllactate is an important competing channel not resolved as a separate node here.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative aromatic-substrate extension of Kaur et al. (2024), who demonstrated H2-driven reductive amination on other keto acids but did not test 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate. Nickel is selected because the cited chemistry demonstrates H2 activation and lower ammonia requirements, not because a natural catalyst with identical performance is known. Neither its reported aliphatic yields nor selectivities can be assigned to tyrosine. Aromatic precursor availability remains unresolved.

reactions.name: Conditional cyanide-mediated conversion of 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate to hydantoin

conditions.other: Proposed pH approximately 8.5 with concentrated bicarbonate buffer, around 0.5 M as a laboratory analogue; ammonia and cyanide available. Buffer is not treated as a demonstrated natural concentration.

reactions.mechanism: Proposed keto-acid-specific cyanide/ammonia reaction manifold involving carbon–nitrogen bond formation, internal redox chemistry, and hydantoin cyclization. The displayed equation is a formal net conversion and does not specify carbon-atom mapping.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative extension of Pulletikurti et al. (2022), who obtained hydantoins and amino acids from nonaromatic alpha-keto acids. This must not be confused with simply applying conventional Bucherer–Bergs chemistry to an unreduced keto acid and assuming the correct hydantoin follows. Formation of this particular 5-(4-hydroxybenzyl)hydantoin, its mechanism, and its yield all require experimental verification. The aromatic precursor remains an explicit unsupported supply assumption.

reactions.name: Conditional hydrolysis of 5-(4-hydroxybenzyl)hydantoin
agents: Hydroxide ions for base-assisted hydantoin hydrolysis

conditions.other: Proposed alkaline hydrolysis stage, initially screening pH 10–12; this pH range is a scenario rather than a reported optimum for the aromatic hydantoin.

reactions.mechanism: Ring opening gives an N-carbamoyl amino-acid intermediate, followed by hydrolysis to tyrosine, ammonia, and carbon dioxide/carbonate.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative aromatic extension of hydantoin hydrolysis demonstrated for other substrates by Pulletikurti et al. (2022), including hydrolysis at 80 °C. Their substrate-dependent amino-acid recovery shows that high hydantoin yield does not guarantee high final amino-acid yield. The required alkalinity, reaction time, intermediate accumulation, and tyrosine recovery are unmeasured here.

reactions.name: Alanine-driven decarboxylative nitrogen transfer to phenylpyruvate

conditions.other: Transient boiling or reflux-like geothermal compartment under an oxygen-free atmosphere; approximately 0.1 M reactants, initial pH 1.9–2.6, and about 5 h as the laboratory reference conditions.

reactions.mechanism: A donor–acceptor imine manifold permits decarboxylative nitrogen transfer from alanine to phenylpyruvate. Acetaldehyde and CO2 are the expected alanine-derived balancing products; this is not ordinary alanine-to-pyruvate transamination.
reactions.reasoning: Bishop, Cross & Waddell (1997) reported phenylalanine formation from alanine and phenylpyruvic acid within a set of low-yield, approximately 1–3%, direct transamination reactions involving decarboxylation. The boiling condition is assigned to the variable-temperature Biochemical category rather than misreported as a 300–370 K surface-pool experiment. Natural achievement of the concentrations and precursor supply remains uncertain.

reactions.name: Conditional alanine-driven decarboxylative nitrogen transfer to 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate

conditions.other: Oxygen-free transient boiling compartment; proposed approximately 0.1 M reactants, initial pH 1.9–2.6, and approximately 5 h, transferred from the phenylpyruvate analogue.

reactions.mechanism: Proposed imine-mediated, decarboxylative transfer of alanine nitrogen to the aromatic keto acid, yielding tyrosine together with acetaldehyde and CO2.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative para-hydroxylated-substrate extension of Bishop, Cross & Waddell (1997). Their phenylpyruvate result supports the reaction concept but does not establish activity or yield with 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate. Thermal degradation, phenolic side reactions, and low intrinsic conversion may dominate. No pyridoxal or enzyme is assumed, and the missing prebiotic origin of the acceptor remains unresolved.

reactions.name: Strecker preparation of the alanine nitrogen-donor precursor

conditions.pressure: Approximately 1 atm in a covered, gas-retaining pool
conditions.other: Proposed pH 8–9; concentrated acetaldehyde, ammonia, and cyanide. Acetaldehyde may be externally supplied or recovered from the nitrogen-transfer reactions.

reactions.mechanism: Acetaldehyde–ammonia condensation followed by cyanide addition gives racemic 2-aminopropanenitrile.
reactions.reasoning: The acetaldehyde Strecker synthesis is established laboratory chemistry (Strecker, 1850); the supplied report also supports the analogous aldehyde-to-aminonitrile logic for aromatic substrates (Friedmann & Miller, 1969). Its operation at the proposed natural concentrations and residence times is speculative. This module is included because alanine is actually consumed in rxn_015 and rxn_016, rather than assuming an unexplained amino-acid nitrogen donor.

reactions.name: Hydrolysis of alanine aminonitrile
agents: Hydronium ions for acid-catalyzed nitrile hydrolysis

conditions.other: Proposed acidic hydrolysis stage, approximately pH 1–2, followed by transfer or pH adjustment before other reaction modules.

reactions.mechanism: Nitrile hydration through an amide gives racemic alanine and ammonia/ammonium.
reactions.reasoning: Established completion of acetaldehyde Strecker chemistry (Strecker, 1850), consistent with the analogous amino-acid-forming sequence used by Friedmann & Miller (1969). The particular natural hydrolysis regime is speculative and requires sufficient residence time. Alanine regeneration from recovered acetaldehyde is possible in the graph but still consumes fresh cyanide and other reagents; it is not a free catalytic nitrogen source.

reactions.name: Conditional oxygen-free radiolytic peroxide supply

conditions.other: Ionizing radiation from a locally enriched natural radionuclide source; molecular oxygen is not a feedstock. Low radical-scavenger loading and physical separation from sulfide-rich reducing pools are required for any peroxide accumulation.

reactions.mechanism: Water radiolysis creates reactive intermediates whose recombination can yield H2 and H2O2. The formal net channel is 2 H2O -> H2 + H2O2; competing recombination and peroxide destruction are not resolved.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative geochemical supply module, not demonstrated or quantified in the supplied research. Standard water-radiolysis chemistry permits peroxide formation without an O2 feed, but the available dose, peroxide flux, and survival in Fe(II)- and sulfide-rich early-Earth waters are unknown. This edge makes the oxidant assumption explicit instead of silently importing molecular oxygen. Its inclusion does not establish that enough peroxide would accumulate for measurable tyrosine production.

pathways.name: Acetylene-derived Strecker synthesis followed by iron/peroxide hydroxylation
pathways.description: Starts from simple feedstocks, but phenylacetylene assembly under the specified conditions and the strictly oxygen-free hydroxylation implementation are uncertain. Sulfur-assisted aldehyde formation and Strecker chemistry generate phenylalanine; radiolytic peroxide then supports the proposed iron-mediated oxidation. Para-tyrosine is only one positional-isomer product.

pathways.name: Acetylene-derived Strecker synthesis followed by UV/peroxide hydroxylation
pathways.description: Shares the phenylalanine-producing module with P1 but uses peroxide photolysis rather than iron-mediated peroxide activation. This is a reaction-distinct radical-generation variant, not an independently demonstrated complete prebiotic mechanism.

pathways.name: Phenylpyruvate reductive amination followed by iron/peroxide hydroxylation
pathways.description: Conditional on an unexplained phenylpyruvate supply. Stoichiometric Fe(II)-hydroxide reduction provides phenylalanine, which is moved to a separate peroxide-bearing compartment for nonselective aromatic hydroxylation.

pathways.name: Phenylpyruvate reductive amination followed by UV/peroxide hydroxylation
pathways.description: Uses the same precursor-limited reductive-amination step as P3 but substitutes photochemical radical generation. It inherits both the unknown aromatic-keto-acid supply and the unverified anoxic hydroxylation conditions.

pathways.name: Alanine-mediated phenylpyruvate amination followed by iron/peroxide hydroxylation
pathways.description: Acetaldehyde Strecker chemistry supplies alanine. Low-yield decarboxylative nitrogen transfer to conditional phenylpyruvate produces phenylalanine, followed by a separate proposed anoxic hydroxylation stage. Acetaldehyde released during nitrogen transfer can be recovered, but fresh cyanide remains necessary for donor regeneration.

pathways.name: Direct para-hydroxylated-aldehyde Strecker route
pathways.description: Conditional on pre-existing 4-hydroxyphenylacetaldehyde, whose prebiotic supply is unresolved. Strecker formation and hydrolysis of its aminonitrile would preserve the preinstalled para hydroxyl group and yield racemic tyrosine without a subsequent oxidative step.

pathways.name: Direct Fe(II)-hydroxide reductive amination of 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate
pathways.description: The most directly supported terminal keto-acid conversion, but not an established full prebiotic synthesis. It consumes Fe(II) reducing equivalents and requires a conditional aromatic precursor together with unusually concentrated ammonia.

pathways.name: Conditional nickel/H2 reductive amination of 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate
pathways.description: An untested aromatic extension of experimentally demonstrated H2-driven keto-acid amination. H2 may be an external feedstock; no dependence on co-localizing radiolytic peroxide with the reducing catalyst is assumed. Supported-nickel availability, competing hydroxy-acid formation, and aromatic precursor supply remain unresolved.

pathways.name: Conditional aromatic-keto-acid hydantoin route
pathways.description: Extends cyanide-mediated hydantoin chemistry from tested nonaromatic keto acids to conditional 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate. Both formation of the correct reduced hydantoin and its productive hydrolysis require aromatic-substrate experiments.

pathways.name: Conditional alanine-mediated nitrogen transfer directly to 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate
pathways.description: Acetaldehyde-derived alanine supplies nitrogen through a proposed decarboxylative transfer to 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate. The phenylpyruvate analogue supports the reaction concept, but tyrosine formation by this route has not been demonstrated and the para-hydroxylated precursor remains unexplained.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The supplied conservation check validates every reaction's stoichiometry. Friedmann and Miller (1969) supports the phenylacetylene/H2S-to-Strecker module, but does not establish this complete acetylene-to-tyrosine sequence under the stated, unspecified Surface conditions. Phenylacetylene production remains the main upstream uncertainty. Anoxic water radiolysis can generate peroxide, and oxygen-free Fenton hydroxylation is not prohibited by the net chemistry, but sustained peroxide delivery and the proposed hydroxylation conditions are not demonstrated by the supplied evidence. Para-tyrosine formation would compete with other positional isomers and further oxidation.
suggestions: Specify the discharge, irradiation or thermal conditions for rxn_001, including phenylacetylene yield, collection and transfer into the aqueous module.
Define the Fenton iron species, loading, pH and regeneration or consumption, and demonstrate para-tyrosine formation under oxygen-free conditions.
Quantify radiolytic peroxide production and losses, including scavenging by sulfide, cyanide and ammonia.
Treat the inferred equal isomer coefficients as balancing bookkeeping, not measured branching ratios; add product distributions and oxidation-loss estimates.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The sulfur-assisted aldehyde and Strecker stages are credible, but phenylacetylene supply is unresolved within the unspecified environmental window. UV photolysis of peroxide is a sound hydroxyl-radical source. However, the supplied research does not validate the exact oxygen-free UV/peroxide conversion, its para-isomer yield or its competition with product photochemistry and oxidation. A balanced peroxide-supply equation does not establish a sufficient environmental peroxide flux.
suggestions: Provide the aromatic-production conditions and a physically justified collection and cooling process.
Specify UV wavelength, photon flux, optical depth, peroxide concentration and residence time.
Measure oxygen-free formation and destruction rates for all three tyrosine isomers.
Justify a radiolytic peroxide source and delivery process that avoids excessive losses in the reducing feedstock mixture.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Phenylpyruvate reductive amination is supported by the supplied account of Huber and Wächtershäuser (2003), and consuming two Fe(II) equivalents is consistent with the encoded reduction. The route is coherent conditional on phenylpyruvate supply. Its weaker components are oxygen-free hydroxylation and the peroxide source. The high-ammonia alkaline amination mixture cannot simply be assumed suitable for the subsequent radical step: ammonia scavenging, iron speciation and peroxide consumption require an explicit compartment-transfer model.
suggestions: Specify how the amination compartment achieves the reported approximately 50–75 degrees C, pH 9–11 and high ammonia concentration.
Define phenylalanine recovery and transfer into a separately controlled hydroxylation compartment, including residual ammonia and iron.
Validate oxygen-free para-tyrosine production and the radiolytic peroxide supply quantitatively.
Retain phenylpyruvate as an explicit boundary input unless an independently supported supply route is added.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The Fe(II)-driven production of phenylalanine is literature-supported conditional chemistry. Replacing Fenton activation with UV/peroxide avoids requiring a Fenton iron cycle, but does not establish oxygen-free aromatic hydroxylation, sufficient peroxide availability or net para-tyrosine accumulation. Transfer from the alkaline, ammonia-rich reducing mixture into an optically accessible radical-generation environment is asserted rather than physically specified.
suggestions: Provide the amination conditions, mineral preparation and actual phenylalanine recovery.
Specify separation or dilution of radical scavengers before UV exposure, together with the associated material losses.
Measure substrate-specific UV/peroxide conversion, positional-isomer distribution and over-oxidation under anoxic conditions.
Include peroxide production, photolysis and nonproductive decomposition in a supply-and-consumption budget.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Alanine preparation is standard Strecker chemistry. Bishop, Cross and Waddell (1997), as summarized in the supplied research, supports low-yield alanine-driven nitrogen transfer to phenylpyruvate under acidic reflux. The acetaldehyde and CO2 coproducts are consistent with the proposed decarboxylative transfer rather than conventional reversible transamination. The Biochemical label does not specify the necessary physical conditions. Low phenylalanine recovery followed by nonselective, unverified oxygen-free hydroxylation makes overall para-tyrosine production uncertain.
suggestions: Specify the reported approximately 0.1 M reactants, pH 1.9–2.6 and five-hour reflux conditions for rxn_015, or justify alternatives.
Estimate material recovery through the reported 1–3% nitrogen-transfer yield and the subsequent hydroxylation stage.
Describe transfers and pH changes between alanine synthesis, acidic nitrogen transfer and peroxide treatment.
Demonstrate net para-tyrosine accumulation under the proposed anoxic radical conditions.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This is a chemically credible conditional route from the supplied para-hydroxylated aldehyde. Strecker addition followed by aminonitrile hydrolysis preserves the required para substitution and is consistent with racemic tyrosine. The supplied research does not demonstrate this exact substrate-specific sequence or establish environmental availability of the aldehyde. Neither limitation makes the graph disconnected, but actual conditions, aldehyde stability and competing cyanohydrin or condensation chemistry remain unquantified.
suggestions: Provide substrate-specific experimental support for aminonitrile formation and its hydrolysis.
Specify separate formation and hydrolysis conditions, including pH, temperature, concentrations and reaction times.
Measure aldehyde survival and competing products rather than assuming quantitative passage through the Strecker intermediate.
Keep aldehyde supply explicitly conditional and distinguish this route from the incompletely characterized 1969 tyrosine side-product mechanism.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This is the strongest conditional target-forming pathway. The supplied research attributes nonenzymatic conversion of 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate to tyrosine to Huber and Wächtershäuser (2003), although the quoted yields rely on secondary summaries. The reaction is balanced, Fe(II) hydroxide is correctly consumed as a reductant, and the product matches racemic para-tyrosine without a ring-hydroxylation selectivity problem. Approval applies to the conditional reaction pathway, not to demonstrated environmental supply of 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate or a complete synthesis from simple feedstocks.
suggestions: Attach the primary substrate-specific experimental conditions and distinguish confirmed product identification from secondary yield estimates.
Specify how a Surface compartment maintains approximately 50–75 degrees C, pH 9–11, high ammonia concentration and freshly available Fe(II) hydroxide.
Quantify reductant consumption and characterize the actual ferric solid products rather than assuming a uniquely defined FeOOH phase.
Treat 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate concentration, stability and delivery as explicit boundary conditions.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The net hydrogen-driven reductive amination is chemically sound. Kaur et al. (2024) supports related Ni/H2 aminations, but the supplied research explicitly identifies 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate as untested. Competing reduction to 4-hydroxyphenyllactate is credible and may substantially reduce amino-acid selectivity. Biochemical is not a sufficient environmental specification, and the presence and performance of an appropriate nickel catalyst cannot be inferred from that label.
suggestions: Test 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate directly under the cited approximately 22 degrees C, pH 8 and 6–150 mM ammonium conditions.
Specify H2 pressure or fugacity, catalyst composition, loading, preparation and resistance to feedstock poisoning.
Justify the environmental availability of the actual active nickel phase rather than assuming equivalence between supported laboratory catalysts and natural minerals.
Quantify tyrosine selectivity against hydroxy-acid formation and other substrate losses.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Both reactions conserve atoms according to the supplied check, and the identified hydantoin has the appropriate substituent for tyrosine production. Pulletikurti et al. (2022) supports the broader cyanide-mediated keto-acid/hydantoin chemistry, but not this aromatic substrate. Formation of the exact hydantoin and its productive hydrolysis remain extrapolations. Successful hydrolysis of an aliphatic hydantoin at 80 degrees C does not establish the rate or yield for this substituted aromatic hydantoin.
suggestions: Demonstrate and structurally identify 5-(4-hydroxybenzyl)hydantoin from 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate.
Specify the ammonia/cyanide concentrations and bicarbonate-buffer conditions used to justify correspondence with Pulletikurti et al. (2022).
Measure the hydantoin's hydrolysis requirements, including pH, temperature, duration and tyrosine recovery.
Do not add species merely to repair conservation: these net equations already balance; the missing support concerns conditions and mechanism.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The alanine-supply module is chemically well founded, and the final decarboxylative nitrogen-transfer equation is balanced. Extension of the Bishop et al. (1997) phenylpyruvate experiment to 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate is plausible but untested in the supplied evidence. The existing para substituent removes the need for ring hydroxylation, but neither useful conversion nor substrate survival under acidic reflux has been established. The environmental labels do not explain the required reaction conditions or transfers.
suggestions: Test alanine and 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate under the cited acidic, nitrogen-atmosphere reflux conditions.
Confirm tyrosine identity and yield while measuring acetaldehyde, CO2 and competing degradation products.
Specify transfer and pH adjustment between alanine synthesis and nitrogen transfer, with realistic concentration and recovery estimates.
Retain 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate as an explicitly conditional boundary feedstock.

evaluation.network_feedback: The network has strong structural validity: all 26 molecule nodes and 19 reaction nodes belong to one connected graph, molecule IDs are consistent, and the supplied deterministic check establishes conservation for every reaction with modest coefficients. No mass or charge violation is identified. The strongest achievement is a credible conditional route to racemic para-tyrosine through rxn_011; boundary feedstocks are legitimate graph inputs, not disconnected or chemically invalid nodes. However, the network does not demonstrate their environmental availability or a complete simple-feedstock synthesis. Literature alignment is good in acknowledging the aromatic-supply bottleneck, substrate extrapolations, positional-isomer mixtures, stoichiometric Fe(II) consumption and oxidizing/reducing incompatibility. Reaction-level citation mappings and quantitative experimental support are still missing. Only Surface and Biochemical labels are supplied, so numerical environmental limits, per-reaction conditions, catalyst availability and transfer mechanisms cannot be verified. Declaring separate compartments recognizes incompatibility but does not establish successful material transfer between them. Oxygen is not required by the balanced net equations, but anoxic hydroxylation performance and a sufficient radiolytic peroxide flux remain unverified. Racemic products and positional-isomer coproducts are not inherently failures for this target; uncertain para-product formation and destruction rates limit confidence. Flagged reactions indicate evidence or implementation gaps, not necessarily impossible chemistry. Overall, this is a useful, evidence-qualified conditional network rather than a validated prebiotic synthesis system, and it does not meet the 0.9 network-approval threshold.
